_about: Plain-English rewordings fed to the translator in place of the displayed English, for strings whose wording is idiomatic. The English site is unchanged. Found in real output: 'comes apart' became 'except', 'cost trust rather than money' became 'more reliable than money', 'climatology' became 'climate science'. Each hint keeps exactly the same {{placeholders}} and <N> tags as the English.
miss.alarmsBody: There was no bust, but this model said there would be one. These false alarms make people trust the warnings less, but they do not cause losses. A model that never gives a false alarm is a model that never warns about anything.
miss.missedBody: There was a bust, but this model said there probably would not be. This is the costly kind of mistake: a forecaster reading this got no warning.

ab.fair: <0>Please note</0> — this runs on a free server that goes to sleep after 15 minutes without use, so the first request can take 30–50 seconds while it starts. That is because the hosting is free; it is not a fault.
ab.start: <0>Begin here:</0> Replay takes a real forecast cycle from the archive, scores it with the deployed model, and shows what this system would have told a forecaster on that day — before anyone knew the outcome.
focus.close: Within the bust threshold — not a bust (±{{thr}})
pipe.intro: The last {{n}} attempts by the data pipeline, newest first — each one is a record written when it ran. <0>Refused and skipped runs are also shown.</0> A forecast cycle that arrives too incomplete to trust is rejected instead of published, because a partial rainfall total would underestimate the quantity that causes most busts. A refusal here means the safety check is working.
rv.remembered: the reason this event is well known
ab.svc: Every number on this site is read from a public, documented HTTP API — the same one this page uses. There is no hidden data source and no number written into the page. <0>17 endpoints</0>, checked with Pydantic and described by an automatically generated OpenAPI document, so a forecasting office could load bust risk directly into its own software.
ab.n5: <0>It does not send alerts to anyone.</0> Warnings appear only on this website — there is no SMS, email or push notification, and nothing is sent to a forecasting office. This is a tool a forecaster reads to help decide, not a warning system that acts by itself.
mp.ladderNote: Each baseline is fitted on the training data only and scored on the same held-out rows as the classifier. Skill compared with the long-run average is 0.000 for always guessing the long-run bust rate; higher is better.
ab.cmp: Every baseline is fitted on the training data only and scored on the same held-out rows as the model. Each one is compared with always guessing the long-run bust rate. <0>0.000 means it is no better than that guess</0>; higher is better.
ab.reading: <0>How to read these:</0> ROC-AUC is the chance that the model ranks a real bust above a non-bust — 0.5 is random guessing, 1.0 is perfect. F1 balances how often its warnings are correct against how many busts it catches. Brier is the average error in the probability itself, so lower is better.
corp.title: When the model says 70%, does it happen 70% of the time?
corp.intro: The forecast probability compared with how often a bust actually happened. On the dashed line, the numbers are accurate. Below the line the model is too confident; above it, not confident enough.
ev.title: Is it worth acting on the warning?
ev.intro: A warning is only useful if acting on it costs less than the damage it prevents. That balance is different for every user, so choose yours:
ab.q1: Every weather forecasting centre already issues a forecast. This system does not try to make a better forecast. It answers the question a forecaster on duty actually has at 6 in the morning:
focus.why: the biggest cause across this whole forecast run
miss.title: Where the model was wrong
ab.t4: <0>Even the reference data we compare against is uncertain.</0> Two leading global weather records differ from each other by about a quarter to a half of a bust threshold. This was measured over about 21,000 city-days. We say this openly instead of waiting to be asked.
ab.q4: We call a forecast a <0>bust</0> when its error lands in the tail of that variable’s own historical error distribution — the 90th percentile, computed on training data only. Each variable therefore has its own threshold, in its own units:
mp.errNote: The baseline gives every forecast the same predicted error, the average over the rows being scored, so it cannot tell one forecast from another. Skill = 1 − MAE ÷ baseline MAE. It is the share of the error that the model removes. A positive value is better than the baseline. MAE is the average miss. RMSE is similar but gives more weight to big misses. R² is the share of the variation that the model explains.
corp.foot: {{blocks}} blocks from {{n}} held-out forecasts. They are grouped by isotonic regression instead of fixed-width bins, so the shape comes from the data and not from a choice of bins.
mp.bustBody: A forecast is a bust when its error is larger than this variable's own threshold. The threshold is the <0>{{pct}}</0> percentile of its error on the training data. The value in <0>Bust above</0> uses the error of the ensemble average for each district and day, which is how a bust is judged. The value in <0>p90 error</0> is the same percentile for the forecast of a single member, and it is used only to scale the confidence figures. One member misses by more than the ensemble average, so this value is larger.
